concepts.title: Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The spectrum is the decomposition of white light into its constituent colors.
concepts.content: Newton understood that white light could be decomposed into different colors and invented the term spectrum.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept of the spectrum explains how white light is not a single entity but a mixture of various colors that can be separated and studied.
concepts.recap_md: - Refers to the decomposition of white light into different colors.

concepts.title: Diffraction
concepts.one_liner: Diffraction separates light into spectral components through the constructive interference of scattered light in different directions for different wavelengths.
concepts.content: Diffraction is a way to separate light into its spectral components. It occurs when constructive interference of scattered light happens in different directions for different wavelengths of light.
concepts.motivation_md: Diffraction provides a physical mechanism for separating light by wavelength, which is essential for spectroscopy and understanding the wave nature of light.
concepts.recap_md: - Separates light into spectral components via constructive interference.

concepts.title: Power Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The power spectrum is the light intensity measured at each wavelength.
concepts.content: The light intensity at each wavelength is called the power spectrum of the light. The color appearance of light is determined by this distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: The power spectrum quantifies how much energy light carries at different wavelengths, which is the physical basis for how we perceive color.
concepts.recap_md: - Represents light intensity as a function of wavelength.

concepts.title: Reflectance Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The reflectance spectrum $s(\lambda)$ describes how a surface scales incident light at each wavelength.
concepts.content: The reflectance spectrum, $s(\lambda)$, of a surface describes the wavelength-by-wavelength scaling of incident light, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how surfaces reflect different wavelengths allows us to model and predict the color of objects under various lighting conditions.
concepts.recap_md: - Denoted as $s(\lambda)$, it characterizes how a surface reflects light across the spectrum.

concepts.title: Transmittance Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The transmittance spectrum of an attenuating filter defines the wavelength-by-wavelength scaling applied to incident light passing through it.
concepts.content: The transmittance spectrum of an attenuating filter describes the wavelength-by-wavelength scaling of light. In this model, the incident power spectrum is multiplied at each wavelength by the transmittance spectrum of the filter. This scaling is similar to the diffuse reflection model, where a proportionality constant $k$ depends on the reflection geometry, characterizing most matte reflections.
concepts.motivation_md: The transmittance spectrum allows us to calculate how filters or semi-transparent materials modify the color and intensity of light passing through them.
concepts.recap_md: - Multiplies the incident power spectrum at each wavelength to determine transmitted light.

key_passage.text: The incident power spectrum is then multiplied at each wavelength by the transmittance spectrum of the attenuating filter.

motivation.text: Such wavelength-by-wavelength scaling is also a good model for the spectral changes to light caused by transmission through an attenuating filter.

concepts.title: Fovea
concepts.one_liner: The fovea is a region of the eye where there are no rods and the cones are close-packed.
concepts.content: The fovea is a region of the eye characterized by a specific sampling pattern of photoreceptors. Near the fovea, there are no rods, and the cones are close-packed.
concepts.motivation_md: The fovea is the center of the eye's visual field and is responsible for sharp, detailed central vision due to its high density of cones.
concepts.recap_md: - Contains no rods and has a high density of close-packed cones.

concepts.title: Linearity and Transitivity of Color Matching
concepts.one_liner: The appearance of any color can be matched through a linear combination of three primary colors due to the three classes of photoreceptors in the eye.
concepts.content: Human color matching performance can be inferred from the spectral sensitivity curves of eye receptors. Experimentation has shown that the appearance of any color can be matched through a linear combination of three primary colors. This phenomenon is due to the presence of three classes of photoreceptors in our eyes. Furthermore, these color matches are transitive: if color A matches a specific combination of primaries and color B matches that same combination, then color A will match color B. As a result, the amount of each primary required to match a color serves as a set of coordinates for that color.
concepts.motivation_md: Linearity and transitivity in color matching provide the mathematical foundation for color spaces and the ability to reproduce colors using just three primary sources.
concepts.recap_md: - Any color can be represented as a linear combination of three primary colors.

concepts.title: Color Metamerism
concepts.one_liner: Two different light spectra are metameric if they appear to be the same color to our eyes because they produce the same projection onto our color matching functions.
concepts.content: Two different spectra are metameric if they appear to be the same color to our eyes. There is a large space of metamers: any two vectors describing light power spectra that give the same projection onto a set of color matching functions will look the same to our eyes. There's a high-dimensional space of light spectra, and we're only viewing projections onto a 3D subspace in the colors we see.
concepts.motivation_md: Because human color vision is a 3D projection of high-dimensional light spectra, many different physical light distributions can result in the exact same perceived color. Understanding metamerism is essential for color reproduction, as it explains why we can simulate a wide range of colors using only three primary lights.
concepts.recap_md:
- Metamerism occurs when different light spectra result in the same perceived color.
 - It is a consequence of the eye projecting high-dimensional spectra onto a 3D subspace.
 - Spectra are metameric if they yield the same values when integrated with color matching functions.

concepts.title: Color Reproduction System
concepts.one_liner: A color reproduction system is defined by spectral sensitivity curves that are linear combinations of the eye's own sensitivity functions.
concepts.content:
We can define a color reproduction system by first specifying its three spectral sensitivity curves. We put these into the $3 \times N$ matrix, $\mathbf{C}$, where $N$ is the number of spectral samples over the visible illumination range. The three curves, $\mathbf{C}$, should be a linear combination of the eye's spectral sensitivity curves, or $$\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \, \mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}},$$ where $\mathbf{R}$ is any full-rank $3 \times 3$ matrix. We can translate between any two different color spaces by applying a general $3 \times 3$ matrix transformation to change basis vectors. Note, the basis vectors do not need to be orthogonal, and most color system basis vectors are not.

(see figure: A color reproduction system. Light sensors a, b, and c respond to the input light spectrum $\mathbf{t}$, giving sensor activations $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$. Combinations of those activations drive the...)
concepts.motivation_md: To accurately capture and display colors, artificial systems (like cameras and screens) must relate their sensor and display properties to the human eye's biological response. This mathematical framework allows for consistent color translation across different devices.
concepts.recap_md:
- A color reproduction system is characterized by a $3 \times N$ matrix $\mathbf{C}$ of spectral sensitivity curves.
 - These curves must be a linear combination of the eye's sensitivity curves $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$.
 - Transformations between color spaces are achieved via $3 \times 3$ matrix multiplications.

concepts.title: Primary Lights
concepts.one_liner: Primary lights are a set of three lights whose weighted sum is used to match the eye's response to a given light spectrum.
concepts.content: A color reproduction system measures an input light and produces an output light that matches the color appearance of the input light. A camera with a screen display is an example of a color reproduction system, as the colors of objects in the world are measured, then reproduced on the screen display of the camera. We can match the eye's response to a given light spectrum through the appropriate control of a sum of three lights, which we'll call the primary lights. For the example of a display screen, the three color elements of each pixel are the primary lights.
concepts.motivation_md: Since human vision is trichromatic, we do not need to reproduce a full spectrum to create a specific color sensation; we only need to control three independent light sources to match the eye's response.
concepts.recap_md:
- Primary lights are the basic light sources used by a system to reproduce colors.
 - Most systems use three primary lights to match the trichromatic nature of human vision.
 - Examples include the red, green, and blue sub-pixels on a digital display.

concepts.title: Gamut
concepts.one_liner: The gamut is the range of colors that can be produced by a positive combination of a given set of primary lights.
concepts.content: Because primary lights are restricted to positive values, some input colors are outside the gamut—the range of colors that can be produced—of a the positive combination of a given set of primary lights.
concepts.motivation_md: Physical light sources cannot have negative intensity. This constraint limits the variety of colors a specific device can display, making it important to define the boundaries of what a system can actually reproduce.
concepts.recap_md:
- The gamut represents the total range of colors a specific system can reproduce.
 - It is limited by the fact that primary light intensities must be non-negative.
 - Some visible colors may fall outside the gamut of a particular set of primaries.

concepts.title: CIE Color Space
concepts.one_liner: The CIE XYZ color space is a standard defined by all-positive color matching functions that are linear combinations of the eye's sensitivities.
concepts.content:
A color space is defined by the matrix, $\mathbf{C}$, with three rows of color sensitivity functions. These three sensitivity functions, $\mathbf{C}$, must be some linear combination of the sensitivity functions of the eye, $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$. One color standard is the Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage (CIE) *XYZ* color space, $C_{\mbox{CIE}}$. The CIE color matching functions, the rows of $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{CIE}}$ were designed to be all-positive at every wavelength and are shown in (Figure 1.1.6).

(see figure: CIE color matching functions @cie1931)
concepts.motivation_md: The CIE XYZ color space was created to provide a mathematically convenient, universal standard for color measurement where all coordinates are positive, avoiding the negative values found in some other color-matching experiments.
concepts.recap_md:
- The CIE XYZ color space is a standard based on human spectral sensitivity.
 - Its color matching functions are designed to be non-negative for all wavelengths.
 - It serves as a foundation for defining other color spaces and chromaticity.

concepts.title: CIE Chromaticity Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: CIE chromaticity coordinates are normalized tristimulus values that represent color while removing overall intensity variations.
concepts.content: To find the CIE color coordinates, one projects the input spectrum onto the three color-matching functions, to find coordinates, called tristimulus values, labeled $X$, $Y$, and $Z$. Often, these values are normalized to remove overall intensity variations, and one calculates CIE chromaticity coordinates $x = \frac{X}{X+Y+Z}$ and $y = \frac{Y}{X+Y+Z}$.
concepts.motivation_md: It is often useful to separate the 'quality' of a color (its hue and saturation) from its brightness. Normalizing XYZ values into chromaticity coordinates allows us to map colors on a 2D plane regardless of their intensity.
concepts.recap_md:
- Tristimulus values $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are found by projecting a spectrum onto CIE functions.
 - Chromaticity coordinates $x$ and $y$ are calculated by normalizing these values by their sum.
 - This normalization removes intensity, focusing on the chromatic components of the light.

prereq.rationale: Diffraction is defined as a physical mechanism used to separate light into its spectral components.
The power spectrum is the measurement of light intensity across the wavelengths of the spectrum.
The reflectance spectrum describes the wavelength-by-wavelength scaling of an incident power spectrum.
The transmittance spectrum is defined by how it scales the incident power spectrum at each wavelength.
Metamerism is the phenomenon where different spectra appear identical because they produce the same projection onto the eye's color matching functions.
A color reproduction system is defined by sensitivity curves that are linear combinations of the eye's own sensitivity functions.
Primary lights are the physical components (like pixel elements) used by a reproduction system to match the eye's response.
The gamut is defined as the specific range of colors that can be produced by a positive combination of a given set of primary lights.
Chromaticity coordinates are derived by normalizing the tristimulus values (X, Y, Z) defined within the CIE color space.

overlay.rationale: The text notes that the scaling model for transmittance is mathematically similar to the diffuse reflection model.
The use of three primary lights to match a color spectrum concretely demonstrates the principle of linear color matching.
The CIE XYZ color space is a standardized color reproduction system defined by specific all-positive color matching functions.
